option_description: Controls whether egress filtering rules are applied to outbound recursive DNS queries from internal resolvers, blocking or inspecting traffic on DNS ports (53/UDP, 53/TCP, 853/TCP, and 443/TCP) to untrusted external destinations. When enabled, internal resolvers are constrained to forward queries only through approved upstream paths.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the dns_recursive_query_exfiltration_via_zone_boundary exposure whenever this attribute is false (not input.recursive_query_egress_filtering_enabled). Additionally, a second policy branch fires when both this attribute is false AND txt_record_payload_size_limit_enforced is false, compounding risk. Without egress filtering, adversaries can exploit DNS recursive query paths to tunnel data across zone boundaries via T1071.004 (DNS) and T1572 (Protocol Tunneling), bypassing perimeter controls entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the firewall or perimeter ACL for egress rules on DNS-relevant ports from the resolver subnet. On Linux iptables-based firewalls, inspect OUTPUT and FORWARD chains for port 53, 853, and 443 restrictions.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L FORWARD -n -v | grep -E '(dpt:53|dpt:853|dpt:443)' && iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v | grep -E '(dpt:53|dpt:853|dpt:443)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules showing DROP or REJECT for unauthorized destinations on ports 53/UDP, 53/TCP, 853/TCP, 443/TCP from resolver subnet IPs, or ACCEPT rules limited to approved upstream resolver IPs only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Palo Alto Networks firewalls, use the CLI to check security policies restricting DNS egress from the resolver zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active deny rules for DNS ports (53, 853) and filtered 443/TCP from resolver subnets to untrusted external destinations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf forwarders block to confirm outbound recursion is limited to specific upstream resolvers and that allow-recursion or allow-query-on are scoped.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: forwarders block listing only approved upstream IPs (e.g., internal DNS hierarchy); allow-recursion scoped to internal subnets; no unrestricted recursion to any.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a resolver subnet host, attempt a direct DNS query to an external resolver that should be blocked, confirming egress filtering is active.
how_to_obtain.command: dig @8.8.8.8 example.com +time=3 +tries=1 && echo 'EGRESS OPEN - FAIL' || echo 'EGRESS BLOCKED - PASS'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Query times out or is refused, confirming egress filtering is blocking direct external DNS on port 53.

typical_values: true (hardened environments with tiered resolver architecture)
false (flat networks or legacy deployments without dedicated DNS egress rules)

option_description: Indicates whether internal resolvers or endpoints can initiate DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) connections to arbitrary external DoH providers (e.g., 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) on port 443 without proxy interception or an allowlist. Unrestricted DoH bypasses DNS logging and filtering controls by tunneling DNS inside encrypted HTTPS.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires a dns_recursive_query_exfiltration_via_zone_boundary exposure when this attribute is true AND inter_zone_dns_traffic_monitored is false. Unrestricted DoH creates a covert channel on port 443 that evades DNS-layer controls, enabling T1071.004 (DNS) exfiltration and T1572 (Protocol Tunneling). Because DoH uses standard HTTPS, traditional port 53 blocking is ineffective, making proxy inspection or category-based blocking essential.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check proxy or next-generation firewall logs for outbound HTTPS connections from resolver subnets to known DoH provider IPs. Known public DoH IPs include 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9, 8.26.56.26.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No permitted connections to DoH provider IPs on port 443 from resolver or client subnets, or all connections are routed through an SSL-inspecting proxy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Cisco Umbrella or Zscaler Internet Access console, navigate to Policy > SSL Inspection and verify DoH provider FQDNs (cloudflare-dns.com, dns.google, dns.quad9.net) are subject to SSL inspection or are blocked outright.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco Umbrella: Policy > DNS Policies > Destination Lists; Zscaler: Policy > SSL Inspection > SSL Inspection Rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DoH-related destinations are either blocked or subject to full SSL/TLS inspection policy, not in bypass lists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Squid or similar forward proxy configuration for SSL bump rules targeting DoH providers, confirming inspection or deny policies are applied.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL entries matching DoH provider FQDNs with ssl_bump stare or deny actions; no unconditional TUNNEL or CONNECT passthrough for port 443 to these destinations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From an internal host, attempt a DoH lookup using curl to a known DoH endpoint and confirm it is blocked or intercepted by a proxy.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused, SSL error indicating interception, or HTTP 403/407 from proxy. Direct 200 response indicates unrestricted DoH is permitted.

typical_values: false (when proxy inspection or DoH blocking is enforced)
true (in environments with flat HTTPS egress policies or no SSL inspection)

option_description: Controls whether DNS traffic crossing zone boundaries is captured at resolver or firewall egress points and fed into a SIEM or detection platform for anomaly analysis. Monitoring covers indicators such as high-entropy subdomains, oversized TXT record payloads, unusually high query volumes, and NXDOMAIN storms consistent with DNS tunneling or data exfiltration.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the dns_recursive_query_exfiltration_via_zone_boundary exposure when dns_over_https_allowed_unrestricted is true AND this attribute is false. Without inter-zone DNS monitoring, the T1071.004 and T1572 attack techniques operate in a blind spot — DNS tunneling and covert channel abuse go undetected as no telemetry is available at zone egress points for behavioral analysis.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify BIND query logging is enabled and configured to log all queries at the zone boundary resolver. Check named.conf for a logging channel directed to a monitored syslog target.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A logging channel with severity info or debug directed to syslog or a file path; a category queries entry pointing to that channel.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows DNS servers, check if DNS debug logging is enabled and confirm the log file is actively receiving entries and being forwarded to a SIEM via a log shipper.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Queries and Answers properties set to True; LogFilePath pointing to an active file; MaxMBFileSize configured above 0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM for DNS telemetry records from resolver subnet sources in the last 24 hours to confirm ingestion is active. Search for events with high subdomain entropy or TXT record query types.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-zero count of DNS telemetry records; presence of TXT, ANY, or MX query type entries from resolver IPs indicates active capture and ingestion.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM dashboard (e.g., Splunk, Elastic SIEM, or Microsoft Sentinel), navigate to the DNS data source and verify active ingestion from zone boundary resolver IPs with anomaly detection rules enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Data Inputs > UDP/514 or forwarder inputs filtered by dns_log sourcetype; Sentinel: Data Connectors > DNS (Preview) > Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active data connector status; recent events from resolver IPs; at least one enabled detection rule targeting DNS tunneling indicators (e.g., long subdomain length, high TXT record entropy).

typical_values: true (mature security operations with DNS telemetry pipelines)
false (common in environments where DNS is treated as infrastructure rather than a security telemetry source)

option_description: Controls whether the DNS infrastructure applies a maximum payload size restriction on TXT record responses traversing zone boundaries. TXT records can carry up to 65,535 bytes of arbitrary data and are frequently abused in DNS tunneling toolkits (e.g., iodine, dnscat2) to encode exfiltrated data. This control limits TXT record sizes at the resolver or firewall/IPS level to disrupt covert channel viability.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the dns_recursive_query_exfiltration_via_zone_boundary exposure when both recursive_query_egress_filtering_enabled is false AND this attribute is false — the combination of no egress filtering and no TXT payload size controls leaves the full DNS exfiltration chain unrestricted. Even if egress filtering is partially implemented, absence of TXT size limits allows tunneling tools to operate over permitted DNS paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND Response Policy Zone (RPZ) configuration or named.conf options for max-rdata-size or equivalent TXT record size restrictions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A max-rdata-size directive set to a value well below 65535 (e.g., 512 or 1024), or RPZ rules that NXDOMAIN or passthru with size checks applied to TXT record responses.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check IPS or DNS firewall signatures active on the boundary device for rules that cap or alert on oversized TXT record responses.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active Snort/Suricata rules matching DNS TXT record payload anomalies or size thresholds, confirming IPS-level enforcement is present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Infoblox NIOS or BlueCat DNS firewall policy console, navigate to DNS Firewall > Rules and verify a rule exists that limits TXT record response sizes or blocks known tunneling domain patterns.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Infoblox NIOS: Data Management > DNS > Response Policy Zones > Add Rule > TXT record size policy; BlueCat: Policy > DNS Security Policy > Response Filtering
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active RPZ rule or response filtering policy that restricts TXT record payload sizes or triggers on oversized TXT responses.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From within the network, attempt to resolve a known large TXT record (e.g., a SPF record with maximum string length) and verify the response is truncated or blocked at the boundary.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response truncated, SERVFAIL, or REFUSED for TXT queries exceeding the configured size limit; normal sized TXT records (e.g., standard SPF) resolve successfully.

typical_values: false (most environments have no explicit TXT payload size limits)
true (environments with DNS security appliances or custom RPZ policies specifically addressing tunneling)

option_description: Controls whether the SMTP relay service enforces strict source trust zone restrictions, permitting inbound relay connections only from explicitly authorized zone(s) and enforcing a deny-all for all other zones. This is configured at the MTA level (e.g., Postfix mynetworks, Sendmail relay-domains) and reinforced by perimeter ACLs.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires smtp_relay_open_across_trust_zones whenever this attribute is false (not input.smtp_relay_source_zone_restriction). This is the primary zone-level authorization gate — without it, the SMTP relay will accept connections from any zone, enabling T1071.003 (Mail Protocols) lateral movement and T1672 (Email Spoofing) attacks where adversaries relay messages across trust boundaries by connecting from lower-trust zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Postfix main.cf for the mynetworks parameter to determine which source IP ranges are permitted to relay. Compare these CIDRs against defined trust zone IP ranges to determine if cross-zone relay is possible.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: mynetworks listing only the CIDR blocks belonging to the single authorized source zone (e.g., 10.10.1.0/24 for 'internal' zone only); no entries from DMZ, external, or management zone ranges.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Microsoft Exchange, inspect the Receive Connector configuration to verify RemoteIPRanges are restricted to authorized source zone addresses.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each Receive Connector's RemoteIPRanges lists only IP ranges from the single authorized source trust zone; no wildcard (0.0.0.0/0) entries or multi-zone IP ranges.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Proofpoint Essentials or Mimecast, navigate to relay/gateway configuration and verify inbound relay source IP allowlists are restricted to a single trust zone's address range.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Proofpoint: Administration > Account Management > Inbound Relays; Mimecast: Administration > Gateway > Policies > Permitted Senders
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Permitted sender/relay IP list contains only addresses from the authorized internal zone; no external, DMZ, or management zone IPs are permitted to relay.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the email platform administrator to confirm whether a formal zone-based relay authorization policy exists and review any change management records for relay configuration modifications.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented policy stating relay is permitted only from a specific named zone; change records showing mynetworks or RemoteIPRanges have not been expanded beyond the authorized zone without approval.

typical_values: false (common in organizations where relay is configured for broad internal RFC 1918 ranges spanning multiple zones)
true (environments with enforced network zone architecture and zone-aware SMTP policies)

option_description: An array of trust zone identifiers (e.g., 'dmz', 'internal', 'external', 'management') representing which zones the SMTP relay currently accepts inbound connections from. This is derived by mapping the relay's permitted source IP ranges against the organization's network zone taxonomy. Multiple entries indicate cross-zone relay exposure.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires smtp_relay_open_across_trust_zones when count(input.accepted_source_trust_zones) > 1 — any relay accepting connections from more than one trust zone creates a lateral movement path. An adversary who compromises a host in a lower-trust zone (e.g., DMZ) can relay messages into higher-trust zones, leveraging T1071.003 (Mail Protocols) to move data or establish persistence by abusing trusted relay designations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract allowed source IP ranges from Postfix mynetworks and cross-reference with zone IP allocation records to identify which trust zones are represented.
how_to_obtain.command: postconf mynetworks | tr ',' '\n' | while read cidr; do echo "CIDR: $cidr"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of CIDRs that can be mapped to zone labels (e.g., 10.10.1.0/24 = 'internal', 192.168.100.0/24 = 'dmz'). Multiple zone matches indicate multi-zone relay acceptance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exchange environments, enumerate Receive Connector remote IP ranges and map them to zone definitions using IPAM or network documentation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Per-connector list of permitted source IP ranges. Cross-reference with IP Address Management (IPAM) records to determine zone membership for each range.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Sendmail access.db or relay-domains configuration to enumerate permitted relay sources and correlate to zone definitions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of IP addresses, CIDR ranges, or hostnames permitted to relay. Each should be assigned a zone label by cross-referencing with network zone documentation. Single-zone entries are expected; multi-zone entries indicate exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the current network zone IP allocation table from the network team and compare against all SMTP relay permitted source ranges to produce a definitive list of accepted source trust zone labels.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A mapping document showing each permitted relay source CIDR matched to its zone identifier. The result is used to populate the accepted_source_trust_zones array. Secure posture = single entry array such as ['internal'].

typical_values: ['internal'] (secure single-zone relay)
['internal', 'dmz'] (common in split-architecture deployments with DMZ mail gateway)
['internal', 'dmz', 'external'] (over-permissive, common in legacy environments)

option_description: Controls whether an ingress filter — such as a firewall rule, network ACL, or cloud security group — is applied at the zone boundary interface to restrict which source zones can reach the SMTP relay on ports 25, 587, and 465. This is a network-layer enforcement control that complements MTA-level relay restrictions.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires smtp_relay_open_across_trust_zones whenever this attribute is false (not input.relay_smtp_port_ingress_filter_present). Without a zone-boundary ingress filter, even a correctly configured MTA relay restriction can be bypassed if the network allows unrestricted SMTP port access — an attacker can still establish TCP connections to attempt relay. This represents a defense-in-depth failure compounding the risk of T1071.003 (Mail Protocols) lateral movement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based SMTP relay hosts or inline firewalls, inspect iptables/nftables INPUT chain for rules restricting SMTP ports to authorized source zones only.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -E '(dpt:25|dpt:587|dpt:465)' && nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(smtp|25|587|465)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACCEPT rules for SMTP ports limited to authorized source zone CIDR ranges; a catch-all DROP rule for all other sources on ports 25, 587, and 465.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS environments, enumerate security group inbound rules on the SMTP relay instance to verify SMTP ports are restricted to authorized source security groups or CIDR blocks corresponding to authorized zones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IpRanges or UserIdGroupPairs entries showing only authorized zone CIDR blocks or security group IDs; no 0.0.0.0/0 entries for SMTP ports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the firewall management console (e.g., Palo Alto Panorama, Cisco FMC, FortiManager), navigate to the security policy for the zone boundary and verify SMTP port ingress rules are present with explicit source zone constraints.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Palo Alto Panorama: Policies > Security > Add filter for destination zone = smtp-relay-zone, service = smtp/submission/smtps; Cisco FMC: Policies > Access Control > filter by destination network = relay IP
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one allow rule with source zone = authorized zone(s) only, destination = relay IP, service = TCP/25,587,465; an implicit or explicit deny for all other source zones on the same ports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host in an unauthorized zone (e.g., DMZ), attempt a TCP connection to the SMTP relay on port 25 to verify the ingress filter blocks the connection.
how_to_obtain.command: nc -zv <smtp-relay-ip> 25 -w 3 && echo 'INGRESS OPEN - FAIL' || echo 'INGRESS BLOCKED - PASS'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection times out or is actively refused from unauthorized zone hosts. Connection succeeds only from authorized zone source IPs, confirming ingress filter is enforced.

typical_values: false (prevalent in flat networks or environments where SMTP relay security relies solely on MTA configuration)
true (environments with zone-aware firewall architectures and documented SMTP relay access policies)

option_description: An enumerated value indicating the level of source IP restriction applied to DNS zone transfer (AXFR/IXFR) requests. 'none' means any host can request a full zone transfer. 'restricted_within_segment' means transfers are limited to secondary nameservers within the same authoritative network segment. 'restricted_cross_segment' means IP ACLs exist but permit transfers to nameservers in different network segments or trust zones.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires zone_transfer_unrestricted_between_segments under three conditions: (1) this value equals 'none' — fully unrestricted zone transfer; (2) this value equals 'restricted_cross_segment' AND tsig_authentication_enforced is false — ACL exists but crosses segment boundaries without cryptographic authentication; (3) boundary_firewall_blocks_axfr is false AND tsig_authentication_enforced is false AND this value is not 'none' — partial controls without layered defense. Unrestricted AXFR exposes complete zone topology to T1596.001 (DNS/Passive DNS) reconnaissance, enabling adversaries to enumerate all internal hostnames, IP mappings, and service records without any active exploitation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf allow-transfer directive for each zone to determine if zone transfers are restricted and to which IP addresses or ACL names.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'allow-transfer { none; }' (no transfers permitted) or 'allow-transfer { <secondary-ns-ip>; }' with IPs limited to the same /24 or authoritative segment. 'allow-transfer { any; }' maps to enum value 'none'. Cross-segment IPs map to 'restricted_cross_segment'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows DNS Server, use PowerShell to retrieve zone transfer settings and determine if secondary server IPs are within the same segment as the primary.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SecondaryServers list containing IPs; cross-reference each IP against subnet allocations. IPs in same /24 as primary = 'restricted_within_segment'; IPs in different subnets or segments = 'restricted_cross_segment'; empty SecondaryServers with no restrictions = 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a zone transfer from an unauthorized host (not a designated secondary) to verify whether the server rejects unauthenticated or unauthorized AXFR requests.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response of REFUSED or NOTAUTH confirms restrictions are in place. A full zone listing (SOA, NS, A records returned) confirms 'none' restriction level — fully open AXFR.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Infoblox Grid Manager or BlueCat Address Manager, navigate to the authoritative zone properties and review the Zone Transfers tab to see configured secondary server IPs and ACL settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Infoblox: Data Management > DNS > Zones > [Select Zone] > Edit > Zone Transfers tab; BlueCat: DNS > Zones > [Zone] > Properties > Zone Transfer
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secondary server list limited to IPs within the authoritative segment (restricted_within_segment) or showing cross-segment IPs (restricted_cross_segment); 'Any' or blank secondary list indicates 'none'.

typical_values: none (common in legacy or misconfigured environments, especially internal Windows AD-integrated zones incorrectly exposed)
restricted_within_segment (properly configured environments with secondary nameservers in the same authoritative segment)
restricted_cross_segment (split-architecture deployments with secondary nameservers in DMZ or separate zones, often without TSIG)

option_description: Controls whether TSIG (Transaction Signature) or equivalent cryptographic authentication is required on all DNS zone transfer (AXFR/IXFR) requests and dynamic DNS update requests, ensuring only keyed authorized parties can receive zone data or submit record modifications.
security_impact: Referenced by both zone_transfer_unrestricted_between_segments and dns_dynamic_update_propagation_without_zone_scoping rules. In the Rego policy, when axfr_allowed_source_restriction is 'restricted_cross_segment' and tsig_authentication_enforced is false, the zone transfer exposure fires. Additionally, when update_source_segment_restricted is false and tsig_authentication_enforced is false, the dynamic update propagation exposure fires. Without TSIG, any host that can reach TCP/53 can request a full zone dump or inject DNS records, enabling infrastructure enumeration and trust manipulation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect BIND named.conf for TSIG key definitions and their use in allow-transfer and allow-update blocks within each zone stanza.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'key "<keyname>" { algorithm hmac-sha256; secret "..."; };' and allow-transfer or allow-update referencing that key name, e.g., 'allow-transfer { key tsig-transfer-key; };'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the DNS server directly to test whether an unauthenticated AXFR is accepted from localhost, which indicates TSIG is not enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If TSIG is enforced, the response should return REFUSED or NOTAUTH. A successful AXFR response listing zone records means tsig_authentication_enforced is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For PowerDNS, inspect pdns.conf and zone-specific TSIG key associations using the pdnsutil command to list TSIG keys bound to zones.
how_to_obtain.command: pdnsutil list-tsig-keys && pdnsutil show-zone <zone_name> | grep -i tsig
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output listing TSIG key names associated with zone transfer permissions. Empty output or no key association indicates TSIG is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the PowerDNS REST API to retrieve zone metadata including TSIG key associations for all configured zones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response showing 'slave_tsig_key_ids' or 'master_tsig_key_ids' fields populated with key names for each zone. Empty arrays indicate no TSIG enforcement.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Controls whether a network boundary control such as a firewall, security group, or ACL explicitly denies DNS zone transfer traffic (TCP port 53, used for AXFR/IXFR) from leaving the authoritative DNS segment toward lower-trust or adjacent network zones.
security_impact: Referenced by zone_transfer_unrestricted_between_segments. The Rego policy fires this exposure when boundary_firewall_blocks_axfr is false and tsig_authentication_enforced is false simultaneously, meaning neither network-layer nor protocol-layer controls exist to prevent zone enumeration. Even if TSIG is configured, a missing firewall rule means a misconfigured or compromised DNS server could still serve zone data to unauthorized segments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List iptables or nftables rules on the authoritative DNS host to verify TCP/53 outbound is restricted to the authorized secondary list.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v | grep -E 'dpt:53|tcp.*53' ; nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'tcp.*53|53.*tcp'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules showing DROP or REJECT for TCP dport 53 to destinations outside the authorized secondary IP list. Absence of such rules or a broad ACCEPT rule indicates boundary_firewall_blocks_axfr is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review cloud security group or ACL rules for the authoritative DNS instance using AWS CLI, filtering for port 53 TCP egress rules.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output showing egress rules limited to specific secondary DNS IPs on TCP/53. An empty array means no explicit egress rule; a broad '0.0.0.0/0' entry means boundary_firewall_blocks_axfr is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TCP/53 connection from a host in an adjacent non-authorized segment to the authoritative DNS server to verify the firewall blocks zone transfer traffic.
how_to_obtain.command: nc -zv -w 3 <dns_server_ip> 53 && echo 'TCP/53 REACHABLE - firewall not blocking' || echo 'TCP/53 BLOCKED'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or timeout from unauthorized segment IPs indicates boundary_firewall_blocks_axfr is true. A successful TCP handshake from an unauthorized host indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review firewall or network ACL rules in the cloud provider console or firewall management interface for the segment hosting authoritative DNS servers.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > VPC > Security Groups > [DNS SG] > Outbound Rules | Azure Portal > Network Security Groups > [DNS NSG] > Outbound Security Rules | Palo Alto Panorama > Policies > Security > Filter by destination port 53 TCP
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress rules for TCP/53 should be limited to authorized secondary DNS IP addresses only. Any rule permitting TCP/53 to broad CIDRs or 'Any' destination indicates the boundary is not enforced.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Indicates whether the DNS server has split-horizon (split-view) configuration defined, creating separate zone response contexts for internal versus external query sources so that internal infrastructure records are not exposed to external resolvers.
security_impact: Referenced by ingress_filtering_bypass_via_split_horizon_misconfiguration. The Rego policy fires the exposure when split_horizon_views_configured is false and ingress_filter_enforces_dns_view_boundary is also false, meaning neither software-layer view separation nor network-layer boundary enforcement exists to prevent external queries from receiving internal zone responses. Without split-horizon, a single authoritative response plane serves all clients, collapsing internal/external boundary distinctions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse BIND named.conf for the presence of 'view' statements, which define split-horizon configuration. At least two views (e.g., 'internal' and 'external') must be present.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Two or more 'view' blocks with distinct names such as 'internal' and 'external'. A count of zero or one indicates split_horizon_views_configured is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows DNS Server, use dnscmd or PowerShell to list active zones and inspect whether separate internal/external zone sets or stub zones with view-equivalent separation exist.
how_to_obtain.command: dnscmd /enumzones ; Get-DnsServerZone | Select-Object ZoneName, ZoneType, IsReverseLookupZone | Format-Table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zone listings showing duplicate zone names differentiated by internal/external scope, or evidence of separate DNS server instances per view. A flat single zone list indicates no split-horizon.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the PowerDNS API to enumerate all zones and check for view-separated zone sets or use of the pdnsutil command to confirm view configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zone list showing pairs of zones differentiated by naming convention (e.g., internal.example.com and external.example.com) or separate server instances per view. A single undifferentiated list indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the DNS server management console for view configuration entries in BIND-based systems via webmin, or review separate DNS server instances for split-horizon in Windows DNS.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Webmin > Servers > BIND DNS Server > Views | Windows DNS Manager > Forward Lookup Zones (compare internal vs external DNS server instances) | Infoblox Grid Manager > DNS > Views
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least two defined views with distinct names and match-clients ACLs. A single default view or no view configuration indicates split_horizon_views_configured is false.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Indicates whether the ACL match-clients or match-destinations definitions across DNS views contain overlapping or ambiguous address ranges, which could allow external clients to incorrectly match an internal view and receive internal zone data.
security_impact: Referenced by ingress_filtering_bypass_via_split_horizon_misconfiguration. The Rego policy fires the exposure when split_horizon_views_configured is true, view_acl_overlap_present is true, and ingress_filter_enforces_dns_view_boundary is false. This condition represents a software misconfiguration where split-horizon exists but its view selection logic is broken, making the boundary ineffective. Overlapping ACLs allow external IPs to receive internal DNS responses, exposing internal topology.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all match-clients and match-destinations ACL blocks from each view in named.conf and compare CIDR ranges for overlap using ipcalc or manual inspection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each view's match-clients block should reference non-overlapping, mutually exclusive ACL sets. The presence of 'any', broad RFC1918 ranges in the external view, or CIDR ranges that encompass both internal and external IPs indicates view_acl_overlap_present is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use named-checkconf to validate the BIND configuration and identify ACL definition errors, then manually parse ACL bodies for overlapping ranges.
how_to_obtain.command: named-checkconf -p /etc/named.conf 2>&1 | grep -E 'acl|view|match' ; named-checkconf /etc/named.conf && echo 'Config syntax valid' || echo 'Config errors found'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: named-checkconf prints the full normalized config. Review match-clients entries: the external view should not include any CIDR ranges also present in the internal view's match-clients. Errors or 'any' in the external view indicate overlap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send DNS queries from a known external IP address and a known internal IP address and compare responses to detect if both receive the same (internal) zone data, indicating ACL overlap.
how_to_obtain.command: dig @<dns_server_ip> internal-host.corp.example.com A ; # Run from external IP and compare output with query from internal IP
how_to_obtain.expected_output: External IP queries should receive NXDOMAIN or a sanitized external response. If an external IP receives the same internal A record response as an internal IP, view_acl_overlap_present is effectively true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review DNS query logs for unexpected external source IPs receiving responses that include internal hostnames or RFC1918 addresses, indicating view ACL leakage.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'query.*IN A' /var/log/named/queries.log | awk '{print $5, $8}' | grep -v '^10\.' | grep -v '^172\.' | grep -v '^192\.168' | head -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing external source IPs (non-RFC1918) querying and receiving responses for internal-only hostnames indicate ACL overlap is causing view boundary leakage.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Indicates whether network ingress filtering (firewall, ACL, or security group) actively restricts DNS queries on port 53 (UDP and TCP) to ensure external source IP addresses cannot reach the internal-facing DNS resolver or its zone data, enforcing the view boundary at the network layer.
security_impact: Referenced by ingress_filtering_bypass_via_split_horizon_misconfiguration in two Rego policy conditions: first, when split-horizon is configured with ACL overlap but no ingress filter compensates; second, when split-horizon is not configured at all and no ingress filter provides an equivalent boundary. Without this control, any external host that can route to the internal resolver bypasses both software-layer view separation and creates a single point of failure for zone data exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check host-based firewall rules on the internal DNS resolver to confirm UDP/53 and TCP/53 ingress is restricted to authorized internal source ranges only.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: INPUT rules showing ACCEPT for UDP/TCP dport 53 only from internal CIDR ranges (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8) and DROP/REJECT for all others. Broad ACCEPT for any source on port 53 indicates ingress_filter_enforces_dns_view_boundary is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review AWS Network ACL rules for the subnet hosting the internal DNS resolver, confirming inbound port 53 from external CIDRs is explicitly denied.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filters 'Name=association.subnet-id,Values=<subnet-id>' --query 'NetworkAcls[*].Entries[?Protocol==`17` || Protocol==`6`]' --output json | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NACL entries showing DENY rules for port 53 UDP/TCP from 0.0.0.0/0 or external CIDR ranges, with ALLOW rules only for internal source CIDRs. Missing deny rules indicate the filter is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a DNS query from a simulated external IP (or from a host in an external-facing segment) directly to the internal resolver's IP to test reachability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A timeout or connection refused response from the external source indicates the ingress filter is enforcing the boundary (true). A valid DNS response from the internal resolver to an external source indicates ingress_filter_enforces_dns_view_boundary is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review security group inbound rules for the internal DNS resolver instance in the cloud provider console, verifying that port 53 ingress is scoped to internal VPC or private CIDRs only.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Instances > [DNS Resolver] > Security > Security Groups > Inbound Rules | Azure Portal > Virtual Machines > [DNS VM] > Networking > Inbound Port Rules | GCP Console > VPC Network > Firewall Rules > Filter by target tag of DNS resolver
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Inbound rules for port 53 UDP and TCP should show source CIDR limited to internal VPC ranges (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8). Any rule permitting 0.0.0.0/0 or external public CIDRs on port 53 means this attribute is false.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Indicates whether the service account or API credentials used by DNS and email services are scoped to operate within a single trust zone or are shared across multiple trust zones, which directly determines the blast radius of a credential compromise event.
security_impact: Referenced by service_account_credential_propagation_across_zones. The Rego policy fires this exposure in two conditions: when credential_zone_scope is 'multi_zone' and cross-zone reuse prevention is absent, and when credential_zone_scope is 'multi_zone' and per-zone rotation is absent. An 'unknown' scope also triggers the exposure when reuse prevention is missing, because unverified credential scope defaults to the worst-case assumption. Multi-zone credentials allow a compromise in a lower-trust zone (e.g., DMZ email relay) to provide authenticated access to higher-trust zone services.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate IAM service accounts used by DNS and email services and inspect their role bindings across projects or resource hierarchies to determine if bindings exist in multiple zones.
how_to_obtain.command: gcloud iam service-accounts list --filter='email~dns\|email~mail\|email~smtp' --format='value(email)' | xargs -I{} gcloud projects get-iam-policy <project> --flatten='bindings[].members' --filter='bindings.members:{}'  --format='table(bindings.role)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Role bindings should show the service account is bound only within resources of a single trust zone. Bindings appearing across multiple projects representing different trust zones (DMZ, internal, management) indicate multi_zone scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Kubernetes service account configurations and RBAC bindings for DNS and email pods to determine if the same service account name or token is mounted in pods across multiple namespaces representing different trust zones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing DNS/email pods using distinct service accounts per namespace. The same service account name appearing across namespaces that represent different trust zones (e.g., dmz and internal) indicates multi_zone scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview DNS and email service administrators to determine if shared API keys, service account JSON files, or certificates are distributed to services in more than one network zone.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review service account inventory documentation, secret management vault policies (e.g., HashiCorp Vault path ACLs), and credential distribution procedures. Ask: 'Is the same service account or API key used by services in both the DMZ and the internal network?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or verbal confirmation that each trust zone (DMZ, internal, management) uses distinct non-shared credentials for DNS and email services. Any confirmation of shared credentials across zones indicates multi_zone scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect DNS server configuration files and email MTA configurations for credential or API key references, then cross-reference those identities against IAM or LDAP group memberships spanning multiple zones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each service's credential reference should point to a distinct identity. If the same keyfile path or account name appears in both DNS and email configurations spanning different zones, credential_zone_scope is likely multi_zone.

typical_values: single_zone
multi_zone
unknown

option_description: Controls whether a technical control such as workload identity binding, network policy enforcement, token audience restriction, or IP-bound token validation actively prevents credentials issued in one trust zone from being accepted or reused in a different trust zone.
security_impact: Referenced by service_account_credential_propagation_across_zones. The Rego policy fires the exposure when credential_zone_scope is 'multi_zone' or 'unknown' and cross_zone_credential_reuse_enforced_prevention is false. This attribute represents the compensating control that can mitigate multi-zone credential scope risks. Without it, a stolen credential from the DMZ email relay can be replayed against internal DNS management APIs or higher-trust service endpoints, enabling lateral movement via trust propagation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Kubernetes network policies and service mesh authorization policies (e.g., Istio AuthorizationPolicy) to confirm that service accounts from one namespace are rejected when attempting to access services in a different trust-zone namespace.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicies --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A 10 'principals\|source\|namespaceSelector' ; kubectl get networkpolicies --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A 5 'namespaceSelector'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AuthorizationPolicy resources with source principal restrictions scoped to specific namespace trust zones. NetworkPolicy ingress rules using namespaceSelector to restrict cross-namespace traffic. Absence of these policies indicates cross_zone_credential_reuse_enforced_prevention is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that cloud workload identity tokens include audience restrictions that limit acceptance to endpoints within a single zone by inspecting token claims and service account impersonation policies.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' 'http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token' | python3 -c "import sys,json,base64; t=json.load(sys.stdin)['access_token']; p=t.split('.')[1]+'=='; print(json.dumps(json.loads(base64.b64decode(p)), indent=2))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Token claims showing an 'aud' (audience) field restricted to a specific service or zone endpoint. A broad audience or absence of audience restriction indicates tokens could be replayed cross-zone, meaning this control is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review HashiCorp Vault policy files and auth method role definitions to confirm that tokens are bound to specific IP CIDR ranges or entity aliases that prevent cross-zone reuse.
how_to_obtain.command: vault policy list | xargs -I{} vault policy read {} | grep -E 'bound_cidrs|token_bound_cidrs|allowed_policies' ; vault read auth/kubernetes/role/<role_name> | grep -E 'bound_service_account_namespaces|token_bound_cidrs'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vault role definitions showing 'token_bound_cidrs' limiting token validity to the originating zone's IP range, and 'bound_service_account_namespaces' scoped to the specific trust zone namespace. Absence of these bindings indicates the prevention is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review service mesh configuration documentation and zero-trust policy frameworks to confirm mutual TLS and workload identity attestation prevents cross-zone credential acceptance.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Istio > Security > Authorization Policies | Consul > Intentions | AWS IAM > Condition Keys (aws:SourceVpc, aws:SourceVpce) in resource-based policies | Azure > Managed Identity > Federated Identity Credentials
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Technical controls documentation showing that service-to-service authentication uses zone-scoped workload identities with cryptographic attestation that cannot be replayed outside the originating zone.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Controls whether DNS and email service credentials are rotated on independent schedules and through independent processes for each trust zone, ensuring that rotating or revoking a credential in one zone does not leave the same credential valid in another zone, and that a zone-specific compromise triggers only that zone's credential rotation.
security_impact: Referenced by service_account_credential_propagation_across_zones. The Rego policy fires the exposure when credential_zone_scope is 'multi_zone' and credential_rotation_independent_per_zone is false. This condition captures the scenario where even if credential scope is acknowledged as multi-zone, the operational safeguard of independent rotation is absent, meaning a compromised credential persists valid across all zones until centrally rotated. Independent per-zone rotation limits the validity window of a stolen credential to the compromised zone's rotation cycle.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect HashiCorp Vault dynamic secrets role configurations and lease TTL settings for DNS and email service roles across each zone to verify independently scoped rotation policies.
how_to_obtain.command: vault list secret/dns/ ; vault list secret/email/ ; vault read database/roles/dns-internal-zone ; vault read database/roles/dns-dmz-zone ; vault read aws/roles/email-internal ; vault read aws/roles/email-dmz
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Separate Vault roles per zone (e.g., dns-internal-zone, dns-dmz-zone) with independent TTL and rotation configurations. A single shared role used across zones indicates credential_rotation_independent_per_zone is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Kubernetes secret rotation jobs and CronJob definitions to confirm separate rotation jobs exist per namespace/trust-zone for DNS and email service account tokens.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get cronjobs --all-namespaces | grep -E 'rotate\|renew\|secret' ; kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces | grep -E 'dns\|mail\|smtp' | awk '{print $1, $2}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CronJob entries showing distinct rotation jobs targeting DNS and email secrets in each namespace independently (e.g., rotate-dns-secrets-dmz, rotate-dns-secrets-internal). A single rotation job targeting shared secrets across namespaces indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review credential lifecycle management procedures, runbooks, and automation scripts to determine if the rotation procedure for zone A explicitly excludes zone B credentials, and whether rotation is triggered independently per zone.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review secret management runbooks, Ansible playbooks (grep for credential rotation tasks), Terraform modules managing IAM/service account keys, and incident response procedures. Ask: 'If the DMZ email credential is compromised, does the rotation procedure only rotate the DMZ credential or all zones?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented procedures showing separate rotation scripts, playbooks, or automation pipelines per trust zone. Evidence of a single unified rotation procedure covering all zones indicates credential_rotation_independent_per_zone is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the cloud provider IAM API to retrieve the creation time and last rotation time of service account keys for DNS and email services per zone, comparing rotation timestamps for independence.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam list-access-keys --user-name <dns-dmz-service-user> ; aws iam list-access-keys --user-name <dns-internal-service-user> ; aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id <key-id>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Distinct access key IDs with independent creation and rotation timestamps for each zone's service user. Identical key IDs or synchronized rotation timestamps across zone service users indicates credentials are not independently rotated.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Controls whether an enforced network boundary exists between the management plane and the service plane for DNS/email infrastructure, implemented via separate VLANs, firewall zone rules, or ACLs preventing direct reachability between management interfaces and service-plane hosts.
security_impact: The Rego rule management_plane_reachability_from_service_zone fires when management_service_plane_isolated evaluates inconsistently (null or absent), indicating no enforced boundary. Without this isolation, a compromised DNS or email service host can reach management interfaces on ports 22, 443, 8080, and 8443 directly, enabling lateral movement from the service zone into the administrative trust zone without crossing any enforced control boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query firewall zone-to-zone policy to verify whether service-plane CIDRs can reach management-plane ports directly.
how_to_obtain.command: show access-list | grep -E '(permit|deny).*tcp.*(22|443|8080|8443)' # Cisco IOS; or: iptables -L -n -v | grep -E '(ACCEPT|DROP).*(22|443|8080|8443)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All rules from service-plane CIDRs to management ports should be explicit DENY entries with no permit rules bypassing zone enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect VLAN and interface binding configuration to confirm management and service interfaces occupy separate VLANs with no shared CIDR.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Management interface bound to a distinct VLAN ID and CIDR block from any DNS/email service interface.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the firewall management console (e.g., Palo Alto Panorama, Fortinet FortiManager, pfSense), navigate to Policies > Security and filter rules between the service zone and management zone to confirm deny-by-default with no permit rules to management ports.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Firewall Console > Policies > Security > Filter by Source Zone: service_zone, Destination Zone: mgmt_zone
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No permit rules visible for destination ports 22, 443, 8080, or 8443 from service zone to management zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TCP connection from a service-plane host to the management interface IP on port 22 to verify reachability is blocked.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or filtered for all management ports, confirming the boundary enforcement is active.

typical_values: true
false
null (unconfigured)

option_description: Controls whether dynamic DNS update ACLs per RFC 2136 are defined at the individual zone level rather than globally, ensuring that allow-update or update-policy directives restrict which source IPs or TSIG keys may modify each specific zone independently.
security_impact: The Rego rule dns_dynamic_update_propagation_without_zone_scoping fires when dynamic_update_acl_zone_scoped is false, meaning a global allow-update policy permits clients from any trust zone to modify records in any zone. This enables record poisoning where a lower-trust host injects or modifies DNS records that resolve services in higher-trust zones, manipulating trust propagation without crossing a boundary control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect named.conf (BIND) for allow-update and update-policy directives at both the global options block and per-zone blocks to determine scoping level.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each zone block should contain its own allow-update or update-policy directive. No allow-update in the global options block, or global set to 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows DNS Server, use PowerShell to enumerate per-zone dynamic update settings and confirm they are not all set to the same permissive global value.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-DnsServerZone | Select-Object ZoneName, DynamicUpdate, IsAutoCreated | Format-Table -AutoSize
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each zone shows an explicit DynamicUpdate value (None, Secure, or NonsecureAndSecure) with Secure being per-zone enforced; no zone should show NonsecureAndSecure without an accompanying ACL.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Windows DNS Manager, right-click each forward zone, select Properties, and review the Dynamic updates dropdown to verify each zone has an appropriate and individually configured setting.
how_to_obtain.navigation: DNS Manager > Forward Lookup Zones > [Zone Name] > Properties > General > Dynamic updates
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each production zone is set to 'Secure only' with Active Directory-integrated ACLs, not a blanket global policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview DNS administrators to determine whether a zone update ACL policy document exists and whether onboarding new zones requires per-zone ACL definition as part of the provisioning workflow.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented procedure requiring per-zone allow-update or update-policy ACL configuration at zone creation time, with review records.

typical_values: false (global policy common in legacy deployments)
true (zone-scoped in hardened environments)

option_description: Controls whether dynamic DNS update requests are filtered at the network perimeter or DNS server ACL level to permit only source IP ranges belonging to the specific zone's authorized same-trust-level segment, blocking hosts from lower-trust segments from submitting update requests.
security_impact: The Rego rule dns_dynamic_update_propagation_without_zone_scoping fires when both update_source_segment_restricted is false and tsig_authentication_enforced is absent. Without source segment restriction, a compromised host in a lower-trust zone can send RFC 2136 update packets to TCP/UDP port 53 and inject records into zones governing higher-trust segment name resolution, enabling DNS-based lateral movement and trust propagation attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review BIND named.conf allow-update ACL entries and match listed source IP ranges against the zone's authorized segment CIDR to verify alignment.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: allow-update entries reference named ACLs whose IP ranges exactly match the authorized management CIDR for each zone, with no cross-segment ranges included.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect firewall ACLs or iptables rules controlling port 53 TCP/UDP to verify that only authorized segment IPs can send update-capable DNS traffic to the authoritative server.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep ':53'; or: show ip access-lists | grep -A3 'permit.*udp.*53'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only the authorized management or update-client CIDR is permitted to port 53 on the authoritative server; all other sources are denied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a dynamic DNS update using nsupdate from a host in a lower-trust segment to verify that the update is rejected by the DNS server or firewall.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: REFUSED or connection blocked response confirming that lower-trust source IPs cannot submit updates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the firewall management API to retrieve ACL rules for port 53 and programmatically verify that permitted source CIDRs match the authorized segment definition.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only the expected authorized segment CIDR appears in permit rules for port 53 dynamic update traffic.

typical_values: false (unrestricted in default configurations)
true (segment-restricted in hardened deployments)

option_description: Controls whether dedicated traffic inspection devices such as next-generation firewalls with deep packet inspection, IDS, or IPS are physically or logically inline on the inter-zone links connecting DNS and email service segments to adjacent trust zones.
security_impact: The Rego rules inter_zone_monitoring_gap_on_foundational_service_traffic fire when zone_boundary_inspection_enabled is false alongside missing telemetry. Without inline inspection at the boundary, DNS tunneling, recursive query abuse, SMTP relay traversal, and lateral movement traffic between zones crosses undetected. The policy treats absence of both boundary inspection and egress telemetry as a combined monitoring gap exposing the foundational service tier.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the network management platform (e.g., Cisco DNA Center, Palo Alto Panorama, or NSX-T Manager), navigate to the topology view and confirm that an inspection device is inserted inline on the uplink from the DNS and email service segments.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Network Management Console > Topology > [DNS/Email Segment VLAN] > Uplink Interfaces > verify IDS/NGFW inline device
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An IDS, IPS, or NGFW device appears as a hop in the path between the DNS/email segment and the adjacent zone, not just as a passive tap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Trace the network path from a host in the DNS service segment to a host in the adjacent trust zone and verify that a known inspection appliance IP appears in the hop list.
how_to_obtain.command: traceroute -n <adjacent_zone_host_ip> # run from a DNS service segment host; or: mtr --report <adjacent_zone_host_ip>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A known inspection appliance IP (NGFW or IDS inline sensor) appears as an intermediate hop before reaching the adjacent zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network device configuration or SDN policy for the DNS/email VLAN to confirm traffic is directed through an inspection policy chain or service graph.
how_to_obtain.command: show running-config interface vlan <dns_vlan_id> # on distribution switch; verify ip policy or service-policy statement
how_to_obtain.file_path: /etc/firewalld/zones/ or NSX-T service chain policy export
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Interface or zone policy configuration shows a service redirect or policy-based routing entry pointing to the inspection device for inter-zone traffic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review network security architecture documentation and change records to confirm that inspection device deployment on DNS/email segment uplinks is part of the enforced baseline architecture.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Architecture diagram and change management records confirm inline IDS/IPS or NGFW deployment on each DNS and email service segment boundary link.

typical_values: false (flat inspection often absent on internal service segments)
true (inline NGFW or IDS present in mature network security architectures)

option_description: Controls whether DNS query metadata including source IP, queried domain, query type, response code, and resolver tier is captured at the zone egress boundary point via a tap, SPAN port, or inline logging agent rather than relying solely on resolver-internal query logs.
security_impact: The Rego rules inter_zone_monitoring_gap_on_foundational_service_traffic fire when dns_query_telemetry_captured_at_egress is false combined with either absent zone_boundary_inspection_enabled or absent inter_zone_anomaly_detection_configured. Without egress-point DNS telemetry, covert channel abuse via DNS tunneling, TXT record payload exfiltration, and recursive query-based zone traversal crossing the segment boundary produce no boundary-visible evidence, leaving the detection gap described in the policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether a SPAN or mirror port is configured on the egress switch for the DNS segment and verify that a sensor is receiving traffic on that mirror interface.
how_to_obtain.command: show monitor session 1 # Cisco IOS; or: ovs-vsctl list Mirror # Open vSwitch; verify source vlan matches DNS segment VLAN
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A monitor session shows the DNS segment VLAN as the source and a sensor or capture device port as the destination, confirming egress mirroring is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM for DNS log sources and verify that records include an ingestion source tagged as the egress boundary sensor or tap, distinct from resolver application logs.
how_to_obtain.command: # Splunk example: index=dns sourcetype=dns_egress | stats count by src_ip, query, record_type, response_code | head 20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SIEM contains DNS log entries with a source identifier matching the egress tap or boundary sensor, not only the resolver host itself.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the network sensor or packet broker configuration to confirm DNS UDP/TCP port 53 traffic from the DNS segment egress VLAN is included in the capture filter.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Capture interface is bound to the egress SPAN interface of the DNS segment VLAN; BPF filter or protocol analyzer includes port 53 traffic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM or NDR platform API to verify that a DNS data source registered at the boundary egress point has received events within the last hour.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A data source labeled as boundary or egress DNS telemetry shows a last_event_time within the last 60 minutes confirming active data flow.

typical_values: false (most environments capture DNS only at resolver; egress capture uncommon without dedicated NDR)
true (environments with Zeek, Suricata, or commercial NDR on segment egress links)

option_description: Controls whether SMTP session metadata including envelope sender and recipient addresses, session IP, TLS negotiation outcome, and message-ID is logged at the network egress boundary of the email service segment, distinct from MTA application-level transaction logs.
security_impact: The Rego rules inter_zone_monitoring_gap_on_foundational_service_traffic fire when smtp_session_metadata_captured_at_egress is false combined with missing zone_boundary_inspection_enabled or inter_zone_anomaly_detection_configured. Without boundary-level SMTP telemetry, cross-zone SMTP relay abuse, unauthorized lateral relaying, and credential harvesting via SMTP session inspection are invisible at the zone boundary, creating the monitoring gap the policy defines.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that a SPAN session or tap on the email service segment egress switch is forwarding port 25 and 587 traffic to a capture or analysis device.
how_to_obtain.command: show monitor session all | grep -A5 'Session.*[0-9]' # Cisco; verify email segment VLAN appears as source VLAN in an active session
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active monitor session captures the email service VLAN with destination pointing to a sensor or NDR appliance, confirming SMTP traffic mirroring.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM to confirm presence of SMTP session records with a source identifier indicating the egress boundary sensor rather than only MTA application logs from the mail server itself.
how_to_obtain.command: # Splunk: index=email sourcetype=smtp_egress | stats count by src_ip, dest_ip, envelope_from, tls_version | head 20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SMTP records in SIEM include a boundary_source field or ingestion host matching the egress tap sensor, with TLS negotiation outcome fields populated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network sensor or Zeek deployment configuration to verify that SMTP protocol analysis is enabled on the interface receiving the email segment egress mirror traffic.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtp.log output is configured in Zeek local.zeek and the capture interface maps to the email segment egress SPAN port.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SOC or network monitoring team to confirm that a defined process exists for reviewing SMTP session metadata sourced from the boundary capture point and that this data feed is distinct from MTA logs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Staff can identify the specific data source in SIEM for boundary-captured SMTP sessions and confirm it is separate from Postfix or Exchange application logs.

typical_values: false (most environments rely solely on MTA logs; boundary SMTP capture uncommon without dedicated NDR)
true (environments with inline Zeek or commercial email security gateway with boundary logging)

option_description: Controls whether automated anomaly detection rules or behavioral analytics models in a SIEM, NDR, or security analytics platform are specifically scoped to monitor inter-zone traffic flows involving the DNS and email service segments, covering patterns such as abnormal query volumes, recursive query abuse, and cross-zone SMTP relay anomalies.
security_impact: The Rego rules inter_zone_monitoring_gap_on_foundational_service_traffic fire when inter_zone_anomaly_detection_configured is false combined with either absent dns_query_telemetry_captured_at_egress or absent smtp_session_metadata_captured_at_egress. Without scoped anomaly detection, collected telemetry produces no active alerts, leaving DNS tunneling, cross-zone lateral movement, and trust propagation attacks undetected even when boundary telemetry exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM or NDR platform (e.g., Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Darktrace, ExtraHop), navigate to detection rules and filter by scope or segment to confirm rules exist for DNS query anomalies and SMTP relay patterns from inter-zone traffic sources.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM > Security > Detection Rules > Filter by tag: dns OR smtp AND scope: inter_zone > verify enabled status and last alert time
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one enabled detection rule exists targeting DNS query volume anomalies or SMTP relay abuse with a data source scoped to inter-zone boundary traffic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM REST API for active alert rules referencing inter-zone DNS or SMTP traffic sources to programmatically verify detection coverage.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: API response lists rule names covering DNS query anomalies and SMTP cross-zone relay patterns with enabled status true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM alert history over the past 30 days to confirm that at least one alert has fired from an inter-zone DNS or SMTP anomaly rule, validating that rules are not only configured but producing output against real traffic.
how_to_obtain.command: # Splunk: index=notable source=inter_zone_dns OR source=inter_zone_smtp earliest=-30d | stats count by rule_name, src_ip | sort -count
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Notable events or alerts appear from inter-zone DNS and SMTP detection rules, confirming both configuration and operational effectiveness.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the threat detection or SOC engineering team to confirm that inter-zone anomaly detection rules for DNS and email segments are reviewed and tuned on a defined schedule and are part of the security monitoring baseline.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A detection engineering runbook or monitoring baseline document lists inter-zone DNS and SMTP anomaly rules with last review and tuning dates.

typical_values: null (not configured in most environments without dedicated inter-zone monitoring program)
true (present in mature SOC environments with NDR or dedicated service-tier detection rules)
false (explicitly disabled or missing)

option_description: Controls whether the mail transfer agent at the zone ingress boundary is configured via transport rules, header_checks, or ACLs to remove or rewrite Received headers and internal routing metadata from messages arriving from lower-trust network zones before forwarding them to higher-trust zone recipients.
security_impact: The Rego rule email_header_trust_inheritance_across_zone_boundary fires when mta_strips_external_received_headers is false combined with either absent zone_trust_classification_enforced_in_filtering or inter_zone_mta_relay_authentication equal to none. Without header stripping, an adversary can craft messages from a lower-trust zone with forged Received headers or internal routing metadata that downstream MTAs and filtering systems interpret as originating from a higher-trust internal zone, bypassing zone-aware spam, phishing, and DLP filtering policies.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Postfix header_checks configuration file for regexp rules that match and IGNORE or replace Received headers from lower-trust zone IP ranges.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries such as '/^Received:.*<lower_trust_cidr>/  IGNORE' appear in header_checks, confirming that received headers from external or lower-trust zones are stripped.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exchange Server environments, review transport rules in the Exchange Admin Center export or via PowerShell to confirm a rule removes or rewrites external Received headers at the zone ingress.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-TransportRule | Where-Object {$_.Name -like '*header*' -or $_.RemoveHeader -ne $null} | Select-Object Name, RemoveHeader, Conditions | Format-List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A transport rule with a RemoveHeader action targeting Received or X-* routing headers is present and enabled with a condition matching external or lower-trust source IP ranges.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send a test message from a lower-trust zone host to a higher-trust zone recipient and inspect the delivered message headers to verify that lower-trust Received hops are absent.
how_to_obtain.command: swaks --to <internal_recipient> --from <lower_trust_sender> --server <ingress_mta_ip> --header 'X-Internal-Route: fake-internal-host' && check received headers in delivered message
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Delivered message headers show that Received entries from the lower-trust source IP and any injected X-Internal-Route header have been removed by the ingress MTA.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Exchange Admin Center or the Exim configuration manager, navigate to mail flow transport rules and verify that a rule for external header stripping is enabled and applied to the connector or receive connector associated with the lower-trust zone.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Exchange Admin Center > Mail Flow > Rules > Filter by: Remove header action > verify rule condition targets lower-trust source IP ranges or external receive connector
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active transport rule appears that removes Received or internal routing headers on messages ingressing from the lower-trust zone connector.

typical_values: false (most default MTA configurations preserve all Received headers)
true (present in environments with explicit inter-zone MTA hardening or compliance-driven header sanitization policies)

option_description: Controls whether mail filtering policies (spam/AV gateways and mail security appliances) evaluate the originating network zone of a message and apply differentiated trust levels accordingly, rather than treating all internal messages as equally trusted regardless of whether they originated from the DMZ, corporate LAN, or production zones.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags the email_header_trust_inheritance_across_zone_boundary exposure when both mta_strips_external_received_headers is false AND zone_trust_classification_enforced_in_filtering is false. Without zone-aware trust classification, a message relayed from the DMZ into the corporate LAN can carry trust metadata equivalent to a message originating internally, allowing adversaries to craft messages that bypass zone-aware filtering and appear to originate from higher-trust zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In your mail security appliance (Proofpoint, Mimecast, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, or equivalent), navigate to the inbound mail policy rules and inspect whether any policy condition references source IP range, connector type, or zone tag to differentiate trust. Look for policy tiers that explicitly segment DMZ-originated versus LAN-originated messages.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Proofpoint: Administration > Email Protection > Policies > Inbound Rules > examine conditions for 'Sender IP Range' or 'Internal Sender Zone' fields; Mimecast: Administration > Gateway > Policies > check for Zone-based policy conditions; M365 Defender: Security > Email and Collaboration > Policies and Rules > Anti-spam > Connection filter policies
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Distinct policy rules or policy tiers exist that explicitly reference zone identifiers, IP ranges corresponding to DMZ vs. LAN, or connector classifications rather than a single internal trust policy applied uniformly.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Postfix-based mail gateway, inspect the header_checks and body_checks configuration to determine if zone-sourced metadata such as originating IP ranges are evaluated. Also review smtpd_client_restrictions for zone-differentiated permit/deny logic.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: header_checks rules that match Received headers containing DMZ IP ranges and apply different check actions, or smtpd_client_restrictions entries that explicitly differentiate subnet-based trust levels rather than a flat mynetworks permit.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Microsoft Exchange environments, review the transport rules (mail flow rules) exported via PowerShell to identify whether any rule conditions include SenderIPRanges or ReceivedFromMessageInfo that maps to specific internal network zones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more transport rules with SenderIPRanges conditions scoped to DMZ or production subnets that apply differentiated SCL values, header insertions, or routing actions compared to rules for corporate LAN sources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the email security team to determine whether the organization has formally documented a zone-trust mail filtering policy that maps network zones to filtering stringency levels, and whether this policy has been implemented in the active mail security platform configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A written policy document or configuration runbook exists that explicitly defines DMZ, LAN, and production zone trust levels for mail filtering, and the team can demonstrate its implementation in the active appliance.

typical_values: false (most common — majority of organizations apply a single internal trust policy)
true (mature environments with explicit zone-based mail security policies)

option_description: Specifies the authentication method enforced when mail transfer agents relay SMTP messages across zone boundaries. Options are none (no authentication, any MTA in the adjacent zone can relay), smtp_auth_plain (username/password credential exchange, not cryptographically binding to the MTA identity), or mutual_tls (bidirectional certificate-based authentication providing cryptographic proof of both MTA identities).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the email_header_trust_inheritance_across_zone_boundary exposure when mta_strips_external_received_headers is false AND inter_zone_mta_relay_authentication equals none. Without authentication on inter-zone relay sessions, any host in an adjacent zone that can reach the relay port can inject messages into a higher-trust zone's mail flow, impersonating legitimate internal senders and bypassing header-based trust checks. mutual_tls is the only value that cryptographically binds relay sessions to verified MTA identities.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Postfix MTAs handling inter-zone relay, inspect the main.cf for outbound TLS policy (smtp_tls_security_level) and inbound TLS requirement (smtpd_tls_security_level), as well as smtpd_recipient_restrictions for SASL AUTH requirements. Cross-reference with transport maps for zone-specific connector settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtpd_tls_security_level=encrypt or higher, smtpd_tls_req_ccert=yes for mutual TLS; or smtpd_sasl_auth_enable=yes with smtpd_recipient_restrictions including permit_sasl_authenticated for SMTP AUTH; absence of both indicates none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Microsoft Exchange, retrieve the receive connector and send connector configurations for connectors that span zone boundaries, and inspect their authentication mechanisms and TLS certificate requirements.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-ReceiveConnector | Where-Object { $_.Bindings -or $_.RemoteIPRanges } | Select-Object Name,AuthMechanism,RequireTLS,TlsCertificateName,RemoteIPRanges | Format-List; Get-SendConnector | Select-Object Name,SmartHosts,AuthenticationCredentials,RequireTLS,TlsAuthLevel,TlsDomain | Format-List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AuthMechanism includes TLS or ExternalAuthoritative and RequireTLS is True for mutual TLS; AuthMechanism includes BasicAuth for smtp_auth_plain; AuthMechanism of None or AnonymousUsers maps to none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From the lower-trust zone, initiate a raw SMTP session to the inter-zone relay MTA and observe the EHLO response to determine what authentication capabilities are advertised, then attempt relay without authentication to verify whether it is enforced.
how_to_obtain.command:
openssl s_client -connect <inter_zone_relay_ip>:25 -starttls smtp 2>/dev/null | head -40; echo -e 'EHLO testhost
MAIL FROM:<test@test.local>
RCPT TO:<user@internal.corp>
QUIT
' | nc -w 5 <inter_zone_relay_ip> 25
how_to_obtain.expected_output: For mutual_tls: TLS handshake completes with client certificate request and unauthenticated relay is rejected with 530 or 535. For smtp_auth_plain: 250-AUTH PLAIN LOGIN advertised, relay rejected without credentials. For none: relay accepted without authentication challenge.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Exchange Admin Center or equivalent management console, navigate to mail flow connectors and review the security settings for connectors whose remote IP ranges span zone boundaries.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Exchange Admin Center (EAC): Mail flow > Connectors > select each inter-zone connector > Edit > Security tab > review 'Require TLS', 'Issued by a trusted CA', and 'Require that the subject name matches' fields; or in Microsoft 365 EAC: Settings > Mail flow > Connectors
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connectors crossing zone boundaries have both Require TLS enabled and certificate subject validation configured (mutual_tls), or have authentication credentials set (smtp_auth_plain), rather than showing no security requirements (none).

typical_values: none (most common in legacy and flat internal environments)
smtp_auth_plain (common in environments with basic relay controls)
mutual_tls (present in mature, zone-segmented environments with PKI infrastructure)

option_description: Indicates whether any DNS forwarder is configured to relay queries to a resolver that resides in a different trust zone than the originating forwarder. This covers scenarios such as a DMZ resolver forwarding to a corporate LAN recursive resolver, or a production zone forwarder targeting an internet-facing resolver in a separate DMZ segment, creating a cross-zone query traversal path.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the dns_forwarder_chain_traversal_bypassing_segmentation exposure whenever cross_zone_forwarder_configured is true AND either per_hop_acl_enforced is false OR internal_zone_resolvable_from_external_forwarder is true. A cross-zone forwarder creates a channel through which DNS queries—and potentially encoded data in query payloads—can traverse zone boundaries.
