Without per-hop ACLs, this chain allows an adversary in an external or lower-trust zone to resolve internal zone names, map internal topology, or use the chain as a DNS tunneling conduit.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On BIND-based resolvers, inspect the named.conf and any included configuration files for forwarders directives, then cross-reference the listed forwarder IP addresses against the organization's network zone IP allocation documentation to determine whether any forwarder target resides in a different zone than the querying resolver.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: forwarders { <ip1>; <ip2>; }; entries where the listed IPs belong to a different network zone subnet than the local resolver's management or service interface — e.g., a DMZ resolver (10.20.x.x) forwarding to a corporate LAN resolver (10.10.x.x).

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows DNS Server, enumerate the forwarder configuration for all DNS servers in the environment using PowerShell, then compare forwarder IP addresses against the documented zone subnet map.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-DnsServerForwarder | Select-Object IPAddress,ReorderedIPAddressList,UseRootHint,Timeout; Get-DnsServerZone | Where-Object { $_.ZoneType -eq 'Forwarder' } | Select-Object ZoneName,MasterServers | Format-List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IPAddress entries in the forwarder list that fall outside the same subnet range as the DNS server itself, indicating cross-zone forwarding. Conditional forwarder MasterServers that resolve to IPs in different trust zones are also flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Windows DNS Manager or equivalent appliance management interface, open each DNS server's forwarder properties and record all configured forwarder IP addresses, then validate each IP against the network zone diagram.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Windows DNS Manager: Server Manager > Tools > DNS > expand server node > right-click server > Properties > Forwarders tab; note all IP addresses listed and compare against network zone documentation
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All listed forwarder IPs belong to the same trust zone subnet as the server being inspected. Any IP in a different zone subnet confirms cross_zone_forwarder_configured = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use traceroute or DNS debug logging to trace the resolution path of a test query issued through the forwarder chain and observe whether the query transits a zone boundary firewall or router hop between the originating resolver and the upstream forwarder.
how_to_obtain.command: dig @<local_resolver_ip> internaltesthost.corp +trace +additional 2>&1; dig @<local_resolver_ip> internaltesthost.corp +norecurse; sudo tcpdump -i any -n 'udp port 53 or tcp port 53' -w /tmp/dns_forward_trace.pcap & sleep 10 && dig @<local_resolver_ip> testquery.corp; kill %1
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNS queries observed leaving the local zone subnet and arriving at an IP in a different subnet range before receiving a response, confirming cross-zone forwarding. Packet capture shows source and destination IPs spanning different zone subnets.

typical_values: false (properly segmented environments with zone-local resolvers)
true (common in environments where centralized recursive resolvers serve multiple zones)

option_description: Indicates whether access control lists (such as BIND allow-query/allow-recursion directives or Windows DNS query filtering) and corresponding firewall/NSG rules for DNS ports (UDP/TCP 53) are applied at every individual hop in the DNS forwarder chain, not only at the initial ingress point. Each forwarder in the chain must independently restrict which source IPs can submit queries and which destination IPs can receive forwarded queries.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the dns_forwarder_chain_traversal_bypassing_segmentation exposure when cross_zone_forwarder_configured is true AND per_hop_acl_enforced is false. Without per-hop ACLs, a forwarder chain that appears secured at its ingress can be exploited by an adversary who compromises an intermediate hop or discovers a secondary entry path, allowing unfiltered query traversal across all downstream zones. ACL enforcement only at the perimeter creates a single-point-of-failure for the entire chain's access control model.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On each BIND resolver in the forwarder chain, inspect the named.conf for allow-query, allow-recursion, and allow-query-on ACL blocks. Verify that each resolver in the chain has its own restrictive ACL rather than relying on the upstream resolver's controls.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each resolver in the chain has allow-query { <zone-local-subnet>; }; and allow-recursion { <zone-local-subnet>; }; directives that restrict queries to only the expected source IPs for that hop, rather than allow-query { any; } or no ACL directive.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows DNS servers in the forwarder chain, check for query filtering configuration using PowerShell and verify that each DNS server has independent filtering rather than relying solely on upstream controls.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-DnsServerSetting -All | Select-Object ListeningIPAddress,LocalNetPriority,RoundRobin; Get-DnsServerRecursion | Select-Object Enable,AdditionalTimeout,RetryInterval,Timeout; netsh dnsclient show state; Get-NetFirewallRule | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -match 'DNS' } | Get-NetFirewallAddressFilter | Select-Object LocalAddress,RemoteAddress
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Firewall rules on each DNS server restrict inbound UDP/TCP 53 to specific source IP ranges matching the expected upstream or client zone, rather than 0.0.0.0/0 or Any as the remote address.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the firewall or NSG rules protecting each forwarder hop to verify that DNS traffic (UDP/TCP 53) is restricted by source zone at the network layer at each hop, not just at the perimeter.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -E ':53|dpt:53|dpt:domain'; iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v | grep -E ':53|dpt:53|dpt:domain'; ip6tables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -E ':53|dpt:53'; firewall-cmd --list-all 2>/dev/null | grep -A 10 'rich rules'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: iptables or firewall rules on each hop's host show ACCEPT rules for DNS port 53 scoped to specific source IP ranges (the zone-local subnet), with a DROP or REJECT default for all other sources, present on every resolver in the chain rather than only on the first-hop gateway.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host in a lower-trust zone, attempt to send a DNS query directly to intermediate forwarder hops in the chain (bypassing the first-hop ACL). If intermediate hops accept and respond to queries from untrusted source IPs, per-hop ACLs are not enforced.
how_to_obtain.command: dig @<intermediate_forwarder_ip> internaltestname.corp ANY +time=3 +tries=1 2>&1; dig @<second_hop_forwarder_ip> internaltestname.corp A +time=3 +tries=1 2>&1; nmap -sU -p 53 --script dns-recursion <intermediate_forwarder_ip> 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Queries to intermediate forwarder IPs from unauthorized source IPs return REFUSED or connection-timeout (blocked by ACL/firewall), confirming per-hop ACL enforcement. If a response is returned, per_hop_acl_enforced = false.

typical_values: false (most common — ACLs typically applied only at the perimeter resolver)
true (present in environments with explicit defense-in-depth DNS architecture)

option_description: Indicates whether a DNS forwarder located in an external or lower-trust zone can successfully resolve hostnames that belong to internal-only DNS zones by leveraging the cross-zone forwarder chain. This measures whether internal zone data (hostnames, IP addresses, service records) is exposed to lower-trust zones through recursive query traversal.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the dns_forwarder_chain_traversal_bypassing_segmentation exposure when cross_zone_forwarder_configured is true AND internal_zone_resolvable_from_external_forwarder is true. Successful resolution of internal zone names from external forwarders exposes internal network topology to adversaries in lower-trust zones, enabling reconnaissance of service locations, identification of management infrastructure, and construction of targeting data for lateral movement. This directly enables MITRE T1599 Network Boundary Bridging and T1584.002 DNS Server exploitation techniques.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host located in the external or lower-trust zone, attempt resolution of known internal-only hostnames through the configured external forwarder using dig or nslookup. Use hostnames that exist only in internal DNS zones and would never be registered in public DNS.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL responses with no IP address returned indicate internal zone names are not resolvable from the external forwarder (internal_zone_resolvable_from_external_forwarder = false). A valid IP address response confirms exposure (= true).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the zone transfer and recursion policies on internal authoritative DNS servers to determine whether recursion is enabled for queries arriving via the forwarder chain, and whether internal zone data would be returned to cross-zone forwarder sources.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: allow-recursion is scoped to internal zone subnets only (not any), and split-horizon views are configured so that external-source queries receive REFUSED or an empty response rather than internal zone records. Absence of view-based access control indicates potential exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows DNS Server, use PowerShell to check whether internal zones have recursion scope restrictions and whether the server responds to recursive queries from forwarder source IPs outside the trusted zone.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-DnsServerRecursionScope | Format-List; Get-DnsServerZone | Select-Object ZoneName,ZoneType,IsReverseLookupZone,DynamicUpdate,ReplicationScope | Format-Table; Get-DnsServerClientSubnet | Format-List; Get-DnsServerQueryResolutionPolicy | Format-List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNS policies (Get-DnsServerQueryResolutionPolicy) show recursive query denial for external subnet sources, and client subnet definitions restrict recursion scope to internal zones only. Absence of query resolution policies targeting external forwarder IPs indicates potential exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review DNS server query logs on internal resolvers to determine whether queries sourced from external forwarder IP addresses are successfully resolved and responses contain internal zone records, indicating current or historical exploitation of the forwarder chain.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '<external_forwarder_ip>.*IN.*A|<external_forwarder_ip>.*NOERROR' /var/log/named/query.log /var/log/syslog 2>/dev/null | grep -v 'NXDOMAIN\|SERVFAIL\|REFUSED' | tail -50; journalctl -u named --since '7 days ago' | grep '<external_forwarder_ip>' | grep -v 'REFUSED\|NXDOMAIN' | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No log entries showing successful (NOERROR) responses to queries originating from external forwarder IP addresses for internal zone names. Presence of NOERROR responses to such queries confirms internal_zone_resolvable_from_external_forwarder = true.

typical_values: false (target state — internal zones should not be resolvable from external forwarders)
true (common finding in environments without split-horizon DNS or per-hop ACLs)
